en: A Brief Exploration of the Internal Meaning of the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, composed by Tàixián.
Now, in explaining this treatise, I shall roughly open two gates: first, to describe the general purport of the treatise; second, to explore the contents within the treatise.
Regarding the meaning:
first, as for the general purport.
Now, the true source is tranquil and void.
It is beyond the scope of cognition;
the nature of dharmas is empty and tranquil,
such that it cannot be expressed through words or realized through cultivation.
Yet, with unceasing great compassion,
the net of his teaching extends across the ocean of suffering to rescue the fish of humans and devas.
The sun of wisdom is impartial;
its auspicious radiance illuminates the dark night,
startling those from their long slumbering dream.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
there will be a bodhisattva whose name is Aśvaghoṣa.
His Way transcends the Three Sages;
his rank equals that of the Ten Holy Ones;
his luminous wisdom is internally integrated.
His compassion extended outward;
he exhaustively investigated the profound essentials and carefully examined the capacities of sentient beings.
He skillfully understood their inclinations and desires;
at the time he composed this treatise,
his composition of it was as follows.
Its principles encompass all scriptures;
its meanings condense all expositions;
its literary elegance is resplendent.
The path of this school is easy to understand;
even if the Buddhas of the ten directions were to praise it extensively for a long duration,
they could not exhaust the merit of contemplating it correctly for the length of a meal.
They can never be fully exhausted;
by this, the Right Path flourishes,
and by this, the Deviant Path declines.
The Buddha-sun shines once more;
the Dharma returns to its former state.
Thus, the Māyā Sūtra says:
Six hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners will arise in competition,
seeking to destroy the Buddha-dharma.
There was a bhikṣu named Aśvaghoṣa Bodhisattva,
who expounded the essentials of the Dharma and subdued all the various followers of external paths.
The second section, "Investigating the Meaning," consists of three parts.
First, it clarifies the classification within the Piṭakas and schools;
second, it explains the title.
The latter shall demonstrate its essential meaning.
Regarding the former, there are two [versions];
there are also three.
Regarding the Three Baskets (Tripitaka):
first is the Sūtrapiṭaka,
which is translated here as "Discourse" (Kīng).
Second is the Vinaya Piṭaka,
which here is translated as "Discipline.
Third is the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
This is called Abhidharma. These three—
Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra— are the means of expression (the signifiers),
while those three— concentration, ethical discipline, and wisdom— are the objects expressed (the signified).
They are assigned accordingly.
As for the two piṭakas:
first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
Second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Regarding the twelve divisions [of the scriptures], they are: the Sūtra (契經).
Geya, Vyākaraṇa, and Gāthā.
Discourses spoken by the Buddha himself (Udāna), Discourses on dependent origination (Nidāna),
and Discourses with parables (Avadāna).
Itivṛttaka, Jātaka,
and Vaipulya.
Rare Dharma. Regarding the exposition of its meaning:
this treatise is subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka among the two Piṭakas.
Among the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka), it is subsumed under the Abhidharma Piṭaka;
among the twelve divisions of the scriptures (dvādaśāṅga-pravacana), it is subsumed under the Sūtra of Exegesis (upadeśa).
Next, regarding the explanation of the title:
"Great" (mahat) takes its essence as the eye and its meaning as that which encompasses.
"Vehicle" (yāna) is a designation based on analogy;
its function is that of transporting and carrying.
Because the Dharma and the analogy are presented together,
it is called the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna is precisely the object of faith.
The essence can constitute the meaning.
The arising of faith is precisely the mind that is capable of believing;
it has clarity and purity as its nature.
The mind and its objects are unified;
hence it is called "Arousing Faith in the Mahāyāna.
As for the treatise:
This is a treatise on the accumulation of righteousness (*jìyì*).
It consists of a dialogue between host and guest,
wherein profound principles are investigated and refuted through successive inquiry.
It is called "treatise" (*śāstra*) because it investigates the principles of correct reasoning.
Furthermore, as for the word "great" (*mahā*):
There are three aspects of its meaning.
First is the greatness of essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*),
which means it pervades all ordinary beings, followers of the Lesser Vehicle, bodhisattvas, all buddhas, and the entire vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
Because it is without increase or decrease,
its characteristic is great;
that is to say, this substantiality is great because it is fully endowed with immeasurable essential qualities (*dharmas*).
Just as the eight qualities of water are not different from water itself,
the third is the greatness of function,
which refers to the two functions of the retributive and transformational bodies.
In the beginning, it can establish the causes and conditions of the mundane world;
subsequently, it can establish the causes and fruits of the supramundane,
continuing until the end of the future.
It is the uninterrupted functioning of transformation.
"Vehicle" refers to this function;
it is none other than Buddha-nature.
The three factors constitute the vehicle:
the Buddha-nature abiding in its own nature is that which is mounted upon,
and the Buddha-nature brought forth is that which mounts it.
Upon attaining the fruit, one reaches the destination of the Buddha Vehicle;
these three meanings—essence and function—are but the single mind in operation.
Furthermore, this is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra*, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, and other such treatises.
Each of these explains seven kinds of greatness (*mahattva*).
Furthermore, there are ten other great meanings found elsewhere,
which are not described here for fear of prolixity.
"Arising" means to initiate.
It occurs because one's own fundamental awakening (mūla-awakening) acts as an internal perfuming cause,
and because of the hearing-perfuming from virtuous friends.
Taking this greatness as a condition,
one gives rise to pure faith toward this sublime object.
Like a crystal bead,
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (She dasheng weishi lun) each explains three kinds of faith,
while this treatise further explains four kinds of faith below.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
First, faith in actual existence,
which refers to [faith] regarding the reality and principles of all phenomena.
Because of deep faith and patience,
there is secondly, faith in virtuous qualities;
that is, within the true nature and virtues of the Triple Gem.
Because of deep faith and delight,
there is thirdly faith in capability;
that is, one has deep faith that all worldly virtues possess the power to be attained and accomplished.
Because it gives rise to aspiration.
Why, then, does the clear exposition of faith not mention other practices?
Faith is the root of practice.
Therefore, it says below:
"One gains confidence in one's own nature and realizes that the mind is delusively active."
One cultivates the dharma of seclusion.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:
"Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of all virtues."
It nurtures all wholesome dharmas,
severs the net of doubt, and brings one out of the stream of craving;
it reveals the unsurpassed path to nirvāṇa, and so forth.
More than three hundred verses praise the virtue of the mind of faith;
furthermore, the Chapter on Pure Conduct consists of one hundred and forty verses.
This clarifies the virtue of the mind of faith (*śraddhā*).
Herein, the arising of faith is explained in terms of the stages of its accomplishment, namely:
entering, abiding, and non-retrogression.
This is because it causes the preceding faith to become rooted so that it is not lost.
Third, as for the indication of its essential meaning,
there are briefly eight points therein.
1. The meaning of taking refuge in and paying homage to the Triple Gem;
2. The meaning of the harmonious integration of consciousnesses;
3. The meaning of the four characteristics.
Fourth, the meaning of original enlightenment;
fifth, the meaning of ignorance;
sixth, the meaning of the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing.
It is also called the five intentions;
the seventh and sixth are the meaning of defilement;
and the eighth is the meaning of the Buddha-body.
The meaning of taking refuge in and paying homage to the Triple Gem.
This treatise consists of three parts:
namely, the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination.
The explanation has three sections:
first, concerning the author of the treatise;
second, concerning the doctrine of the treatise.
Third, regarding the benefit of others,
there are three sections in the first part.
First, the opening three verses of the treatise consist of the homage, the request for grace, and the invocation.
This is the basis upon which the author of the treatise initiates his practice.
Second, the treatise states that from this point downward, he proclaims the correct meaning for the sake of sentient beings;
this constitutes the author’s practice of the gift of Dharma.
The final verse at the end of the third part concludes the discourse with a dedication of merit;
it consists of the great vows arising from the practice itself.
Thus, all three parts together constitute the Master’s illumination of the sun of the Buddha’s Dharma and his conduct and vows for bestowing the gift of Dharma upon all sentient beings.
The remaining two [points] are as explained in the commentary.
The three verses are divided into two parts;
the first two lines of verse clarify the homage to the Triple Gem.
The final line of verse expresses reverence.
This section also has two parts.
First, the homage:
This reveals the utmost sincerity of the one who takes refuge.
Second, from "Exhausting the ten directions" onwards, it clarifies the profundity and vastness of that which is revered.
Within the former [section], there are three meanings.
"Taking refuge once" has the meaning of "tending toward.
As for "life":
One's own life and nature are what all living beings value most;
nothing takes precedence over this.
Now this author of the treatise has attained indestructible faith;
he dedicates his very life to take refuge in the Triple Gem.
This is because it is requested that an explanation be added.
As for the two types of taking refuge (*śaraṇagamana*),
they have the meaning of "reverent compliance."
"Command" refers to the commands of all Buddhas.
This clarifies that the author of the treatise reverently upholds the Tathāgata’s command to transmit the Dharma and benefit sentient beings.
The Three Refuges have the meaning of returning to the source;
that is to say, the six sense faculties of sentient beings.
Arising from the single mind,
it turns its back on its own source and scatters toward the six sense objects.
Now, by raising up the life-faculty (jīvitendriya),
one comprehensively gathers the six sense organs and returns them to the source of the single mind.
Therefore, it is said "I take refuge.
Regarding "throughout the ten directions," there are two meanings.
First, it is not merely taking refuge in the Triple Gem of a single direction,
but rather paying equal reverence throughout the ten directions;
second, within those ten directions, one does not take refuge in only one or two lands.
Furthermore, in each and every direction, there are inexhaustible lands containing all the Three Jewels.
Regarding these two verses,
there are briefly three interpretations.
One interpretation states:
the first line is general;
the subsequent three lines clarify the Jewel of the Buddha.
The next three phrases clarify the Jewel of the Dharma;
the final phrase clarifies the Jewel of the Sangha.
One interpretation states:
The first line refers to the Buddha;
the next two phrases refer to the Dharma;
and the final two phrases refer to the Saṃgha.
One interpretation states:
the first six phrases refer to the Buddha;
the next one refers to the Dharma.
The latter one refers to the Saṃgha.
Now, based on this explanation, we shall clarify the four meanings within the Jewel of the Buddha.
First, according to the three types of action (trikarma).
That is to say: thorough knowledge of mental action,
unimpeded physical action,
and compassionate verbal action that rescues others.
These three types of action are superior;
they correspond respectively to the three phrases.
Second, [they are distinguished] in terms of the two benefits.
That is to say, the first two phrases clarify the virtues of self-benefit:
internally there is the wisdom of universal knowledge,
and externally there is unimpeded form.
The phrases such as "Savior of the World" (*jagat-tāraṇa*) manifest the virtue of benefiting others,
just as a great elder enters a burning house to rescue those suffering from the flames.
Third, [this is explained] in terms of the three virtues.
This refers to great concentration, great wisdom, and great compassion.
The particle "者" (zhě) serves to link these virtues to the person.
It means one who is endowed with all the aforementioned virtues.
This is precisely the Buddha.
"The fourfold clarity" refers here to the two bodies:
the retribution body (*vipākakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Because the Dharma-body enters the Jewel of the Dharma,
there are two kinds of universal knowledge:
first, the possession of wisdom.

The second is conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), which universally knows the distinctions of dependent origination within the gate of the mind’s arising and ceasing (*citta-utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).
It universally knows such things as the ocean-like, *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-sama* merits within the gate of the true thusness of the mind (*tathatā-mukha*).
The principles and means of valid cognition are equally reflected therein,
resulting in non-erroneous, universal knowledge.
Within the second Jewel of the Dharma, there are four [aspects].
This refers to the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit.
These three phrases are divided into two parts;
the first phrase represents the former.
The latter two phrases provide the explanation:
in the first [of these], essence is the greatness of essence,
and characteristics are the greatness of characteristics.
The "greatness of function" (yòngdà) is distinguished as the reward body (bǎoshēn) and the transformation body (huàshēn). Therefore,
the two kinds of greatness— essence (tǐ) and characteristic (xiàng)— are subsumed within the dharma-body (fǎshēn),
because that greatness of function arises based upon essence and characteristic and ultimately returns to them.
This refers to the essential characteristics of that body.
In the following two phrases,
"the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*) explains the magnitude of essence (*tadātva-mahattva*).
Regarding the phrase "immeasurable and so forth," it explains the greatness of the characteristics,
and so on. Within the third [jewel], the Sangha,
the Sangha includes both ordinary beings and sages.
The "Jewel" refers exclusively to the stages of the noble ones (ārya).
While these noble stages encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles,
the Bodhisattva stage is supreme.
Therefore, in this context, one takes refuge solely in the Sangha of the great Bodhisattvas on the bhūmis;
to realize the principle and give rise to practice is called "cultivation according to reality."
"Practicing according to reality" refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
"And so forth" means:
This is the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
It is as explained in the following sections and in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* and the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.
Regarding the second point, the expression of reverence, there are three aspects.
First, to benefit sentient beings;
second, to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not interrupted;
third, to cause the Dharma to abide for a long time.
The four statements are divided into three parts.
First, regarding the person for whom [the teaching] is intended:
they are precisely those belonging to the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi).
Furthermore, these include both those fixed in error and those fixed in correctness;
moreover, all six stages are the objects of action,
which corresponds to the first phrase.
The benefits accomplished therein are twofold:
first, the benefit of abandoning faults;
second, the benefit of accomplishing practice.
This corresponds precisely to the following two lines: because of initial doubt, one is deluded regarding the truth and loses bliss;
because of grasping, one gives rise to false conceptualizations and produces the seeds of suffering.
According to the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), Bodhisattvas contemplate sentient beings in three ways.
Arouse great compassion:
first, they are separated from the bliss of the ultimate truth;
second, they are fully possessed of all sufferings.
Third, regarding the two inversions therein:
the explanation states that true bliss is originally present.
One loses it without realizing it;
false suffering is fundamentally empty.
One attains it without awakening to it.
Regarding those gains and losses,
there is no awareness at all;
therefore, the Bodhisattva has now composed this treatise out of compassion.
This is because, in the section "Establishing the Meaning" (*siddhānta-vibhāga*) where the correct principle is revealed,
it removes doubts, awakens one to the truth,
remedies dogmatic attachments, and brings liberation from suffering.
The section on causes and conditions states:
"Because one is far removed from delusion and pride,
and has emerged from the net of error," and so forth.
Therefore it is said: "Eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments.
When these two are accomplished by the practitioner, they will no longer harbor doubt regarding the Truth.
One does not cling to what is false.
Not yet knowing in which vehicle to initiate practice,
one [should do so] in the Mahāyāna, because it is the ultimate and fundamental Dharma.
One does not yet know what kind of practice should be undertaken within this Mahāyāna;
it is said that one should undertake the practice of generating faith,
for faith is the foundation of all practices.
Therefore, one gives rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna;
this refers to the section on the characteristics of setting out upon the path below,
as well as the section on practicing faith.
This constitutes the accomplishment of this practice.
Third, regarding the intention for beneficial increase:
it means causing sentient beings to depart from transgressions, fulfill their faith, accomplish their practices, and achieve the fruits thereof.
Therefore, it is said that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"Plant the seeds of the Buddha within the field of sentient beings."
The sprout of perfect enlightenment arises.
Therefore, it is able to ensure that the Jewel of the Buddha remains uninterrupted, and so forth.
Furthermore, there is a detailed explanation regarding the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels.
One should immediately encourage the cultivation of the section on benefits.
Furthermore, another commentary states that the general purport of composing this treatise does not exceed two types.
The first half clarifies [the purpose of] transforming sentient beings below;
the second half reveals [the purpose of] propagating the Buddha-way above.
This is why sentient beings remain perpetually submerged in the ocean of birth and death.
Those who do not proceed toward the shore of nirvāṇa do so solely due to doubt and false attachments.
There are two kinds of such doubt.
First, doubt regarding the Dharma obstructs the arousal of the resolve for enlightenment;
second, doubt regarding the gateways obstructs spiritual practice.
Regarding the first: is the essence of the Mahāyāna Dharma manifold or singular?
If they were one,
there would be no distinct phenomena;
because there are no distinct phenomena, there would be no sentient beings.
For whom does the Bodhisattva give rise to the great vow?
If there were many dharmas,
they would not be of a single essence.
Because they are not of one essence, things and the self are each distinct;
how, then, could there arise the great compassion of sameness of essence?
For this reason, the aspiration for enlightenment cannot be generated.
Regarding the "Gate of Doubt":
the gates of teaching established by the Tathāgata are numerous;
according to which gate [should one rely]?
When first setting out on the path of practice,
one may follow either approach; however,
it is not possible to enter them all at once.
If one relies on either the first or the second [alternative],
what is there to abandon or to adopt?
Consequently, one cannot initiate practice.
Now, in order to dispel these two doubts,
a single mental dharma (citta-dharma) is established,
opening up two types of gates.
Establishing "one mind" dispels that initial doubt,
clarifying that the Mahāyāna Dharma consists solely of one mind.
Apart from the one mind, there are no other dharmas;
there is only ignorance,
which deludes its own single mind.
It gives rise to various waves that circulate through the six realms;
although it produces these waves of the six realms, [it remains undisturbed].
Without departing from the ocean of the one mind,
one gives rise to the six realms through that very one mind,
thereby formulating great vows of universal salvation.
Because the six realms do not transcend the single mind,
one is able to give rise to great compassion of identical essence;
thus, one attains the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Regarding the opening of two gates:
this dispels the second doubt,
that although the teaching gates are numerous, [they are nonetheless unified].
At the initial stage of practice, there are only two gates:
one relies on the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) to cultivate the practice of tranquility (śamatha),
and the other relies on the gate of arising and ceasing to give rise to the practice of insight (vipaśyanā).
When śamatha and vipaśyanā are practiced in unison,
all myriad practices are complete.
One enters through these two gates.
Since all gates are accessible,
one is able to initiate practice; thus,
one abandons false attachments.
People cling to the attachment to dharmas.
Those who propagate the Buddha-way above eliminate doubt regarding the two extremes.
They give rise to resolute faith and believe in and understand the Mahāyāna as being solely the one mind.
Therefore, it is called the right faith of the Mahāyāna.
By abandoning the conceptualization of the two attachments,
one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Having been born into the family of the Tathāgata,
they will certainly succeed to the rank of Buddha;
therefore, it is said that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma can be entered through faith;
it can be crossed by means of wisdom."
Therefore, faith and wisdom are cited to clarify the propagation of the Buddha-way and the principle of the harmonious integration of consciousness.
Briefly, there are two sections:
first, an explanation of the five members and eight reasons;
second, a clarification of their underlying intent.
The beginning and middle also consist of two parts:
first, the explanation of the five members;
second, the explanation of the eight causes.
Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned dharmas":
this is a general enumeration of the meaning of the dharmas—
the dharma of one mind, two gates, and three greatnesses.
This is the very essence of the Dharma.
That which can give rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna distinguishes the functional power of the Dharma.
That is to say, with respect to the gate of True Suchness (tathatā),
one’s faith in the principle is decisive; with respect to the gate of arising and ceasing (utpāda-nirodha), [one’s faith in the practice is decisive].
The functioning of karma does not cease.
According to the Great Meaning,
this refers to the indestructible faith in the Triple Gem.
Regarding the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*):
it enters, abides, and becomes a faculty.
There are two types of faculties.
First is the meaning of "ability to maintain," which refers to not losing one's own portion.
Second is the meaning of "producing what follows."
This refers to seeking higher advancement.
Not a single word arises of itself;
every formulation must have its source.
This is the section on the causes and conditions of names.
Now that the two modes of attainment have been established,
I shall briefly set forth their essential principles.
Causing sentient beings to give rise to faith is called the section on establishing the doctrine;
as the essentials of the three schools have now been briefly presented.

The section that extensively explains [the subject] so as to produce understanding is called the "Section on Exegesis. Once understanding has been produced through this exegesis, [it proceeds to the next stage].
To give rise to practice based on understanding,
yet to have understanding without practice—
this is what is not appropriate.
Therefore, there is the "Section on Cultivating Faith.
Although it demonstrates the rules of conduct,
those of dull faculties may become indolent and arrogant.
Raising up [the topic of] benefit to encourage practice,
there is thus the section on the benefits of encouraging the cultivation of practice.
This will be explained later within the exposition of the eight causes and conditions.
The first is general,
while the latter seven are specific.
The general intent clarifies that it causes sentient beings to depart from the three types of suffering and the two kinds of death, thereby attaining bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Therefore, he was able to compose this treatise.

Regarding the first part of the "Distinctive Features," it serves as the causal basis for the "Section on Establishing the Thesis" and the "Section on Exposition" to reveal the correct meaning and counteract false attachments.
If one assigns them to stages,
they correspond to the stage of the three types of worthies within the gate of birth-and-death.
Original enlightenment is called "Suchness" (tathatā),
and initial enlightenment is called "coming.
Initial and original enlightenment are non-dual.
It is called "Tathāgata.
This reveals that what is realized is termed "thus" (tathā),
and the capacity to realize it is termed "come" (āgata).
Therefore, for all sentient beings who have not yet attained the wisdom of the true essence,
this suchness has no coming.
Second, it acts as the cause for those who have set out upon the path.
This corresponds to the final stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
The third [section] serves as the cause for the four types of faith and the four practices described in the "Chapter on Cultivating Faith" (*Xinxing xin*).
This corresponds to the stage of abiding in the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-vihāra*).
The remaining four correspond to the initial stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Among these four, there are the lower, middle, and upper grades;
the final one serves as an exhortation for cultivation.
Among the three grades, those of the highest grade are born in the Pure Land because their faith is perfected.
This is stated in the Section on Establishing the Meaning.
"Dharma" refers to the essence of the Mahāyāna;
its status encompasses both the defiled and the pure.
"Meaning" refers to the meaning of the Mahāyāna name;
this mind possesses three great meanings.
Therefore, it is called "Great.
There are two [aspects]:
that which sets things in motion is called a "vehicle" (yāna).
This refers precisely to the causal vehicle and the resultant vehicle.
"The mind of sentient beings" indicates the essential nature of that dharma.
What is called the one *tathāgatagarbha*-mind contains both the harmonious and non-harmonious dual consciousnesses,
and both abide within the stage of sentient beings.
If one is at the stage of Buddhahood,
there is no sense of combination,
because from the very beginning it is identical with the source, being solely suchness.
Now, within the context of sentient beings who follow the flow,
these two consciousnesses are fully present.
They encompass all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
If one follows along with defilement and becomes non-awakening,
this subsumes worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*).
Unchanging original awakening (*mūla-ajñāna*) and the transformative awakening of defilement (*ādi-bodhi*) subsume supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*).
Furthermore, this demonstrates that the Mahāyāna differs from the Hīnayāna;
for it is precisely because this mind universally encompasses all phenomena,
and the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is nothing other than the single mind.
This differs from the various distinct entities of the dharmas in the Hinayana;
this is explained according to the gate of arising and ceasing.
If one were to explain it according to the gate of true thusness (tathatā), [it would be different].
This immediately integrates and subsumes both the defiled and the pure without distinction;
therefore, it is a universal inclusion.
Within the section on the "Exegesis of Divisions," there are three gates.
1. The gate of revealing the correct meaning (*samyagartha-pradarśana-mukha*), which refers to the correct exposition of the established meanings of the Mahāyāna teachings.
2. The gate of counteracting false attachments (*mithyā-grāha-pratipakṣa-mukha*).
This refers to the gateway of the characteristics of entering the path through the threefold discrimination that eliminates emotional attachments once correct principles have been clarified.
That is to say, by dispelling erroneous attachments to persons and phenomena,
one clarifies the stages of ascending toward the correct path.
Second, to clarify the meaning of "harmony":
first, the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind contains two meanings.
The first is the meaning of the unchanging self-nature that is free from all characteristics.
This is the gate of suchness (tathatā-mukha);
that is to say, it is neither defiled nor pure,
and is without arising or ceasing.
Unwavering,
of equal single flavor,
