These two exist within the stage of the subtle differentiation of the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (evolving consciousness) and belong to the associated mind (*samprayukta-citta*).
Ignorance combines with the signs of the preceding birth and turns that pure mind;
even at this stage, its mode of activity remains subtle.
The firm persistence of attachment to dharmas is called the characteristic of abiding;
it refers to the latter two among the three subtle [evolutions].
Furthermore, these include the first two among the six coarse factors,
the last four among the five mental factors,
and the middle four among the six defilements.
These are all identical.
This is subsumed within the characteristic of abiding.
As for the two aspects of the characteristic of difference:
First is the characteristic of grasping;
second is the characteristic of calculating names.
This refers to how this ignorance is deluded regarding the aforementioned phenomena of defilement and purity, as well as opposition and conformity.
Furthermore, they give rise to greed, hatred, and other afflictions,
as well as the view of self and person; thus they cling to signs and calculate names,
and their grasping becomes increasingly deep.
This occurs at the stage of the coarse division of the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*),
where ignorance (*avidyā*) and the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) are conjoined,
thereby transforming that pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*).
Causing one to reach this stage,
the mode of activity is somewhat coarse,
with the body and speech being distracted and agitated.
Now, these various karmas are termed "dissimilar characteristics" (*visadṛśa-lakṣaṇa*);
they consist of the middle two among the six coarse [karmas] and the first one among the six defiled [karmas].
Together with the final mental consciousness among the five types of consciousness,
these are all identical;
this is their distinguishing characteristic.
Regarding the first characteristic of cessation,
it is the characteristic of initiating karma; that is to say,
because this ignorance does not understand that the two types of karma— good and evil— necessarily bring about the two types of retribution— suffering and pleasure.
Extensively confronting various conditions,
one accumulates all manner of karma;
depending upon that karma, one undergoes its results.
It extinguishes the preceding distinct mind and causes one to fall into the various realms of existence through the power of ignorance.
Transforming that pure mind until it reaches this final limit,
its mode of activity is most coarse.
Reaching this point constitutes the ultimate limit;
therefore, it is called the "characteristic of cessation.
This is precisely the fifth characteristic among the six coarse characteristics.
Since the retribution cannot be severed,
the sixth characteristic is not discussed.
Therefore, the four characteristics within the three realms are nothing but the dream-like mind.
All are due to the power of fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
Thus, a sutra says:
"The power of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) is the greatest."
It is able to universally produce all realms of existence and births.
The Treatise states:
"One should know that ignorance can give rise to all defiled phenomena."
Furthermore, another commentary states:
It is asked, "Regarding these four characteristics herein, are they distinct or simultaneous?
Are they sequential or concurrent?"
If they were simultaneous,
why does the treatise explain the distinction between the four stages of awakening?
If they were sequential, [why would it not be so?]
How can it be that the four characteristics exist simultaneously?
The answer is:
according to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is said as follows.
At the time when these four characteristics are simultaneous,
their four functions occur sequentially; therefore,
there is a distinction in the moments of cognition.
Because their substance exists simultaneously,
they are said to exist at the same time.
The Satyasiddhi school states:
The four characteristics have a sequence of before and after;
however, when primordial enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) is viewed in relation to these four characteristics, there is no before or after.
Therefore, it is said that they exist simultaneously.
The Mahāyāna Secret Teachings state:
"When awakening to the four marks,
there is a sequence of shallow and deep stages."
The four characteristics that are perceived exist simultaneously;
three arise together.
Abiding is the fourth;
change is the sixth;
cessation is the seventh; and the three characteristics of arising are [the first three].
First is the characteristic of karma:
that is, due to ignorance,
one fails to awaken and the mind moves.
Although there is arising and ceasing,
the characteristics and the perceived object are not yet differentiated,
just as when the characteristic of future birth is about to reach the time of its actual application.
Second is the characteristic of transformation:
that is, based on the movement of thought,
it transforms into the capacity for seeing.
Just as when the characteristics of future arising reach the time of actual function,
there are three present characteristics;
namely, based on the characteristic of the perceiver.
The objective sphere has already manifested;
just as the characteristic of future arising reaches the present,
so too does ignorance [arise] together with these three.
Corresponding to these perfumations and stirrings,
the essence of the mind unites with its manifestations,
and the mind follows them in its shifting movements.
Even unto the manifestation of signs:
just as in the Hīnayāna, the future mind follows its characteristic of arising and gradually reaches the present,
so too in the Mahāyāna, the Tathāgatagarbha-mind follows its arising and reaches the present.
The meaning is likewise.
These three are all distinctions within the state of the ālayavijñāna;
they are called the three profound modes of arising.
Regarding the four abidings:
through ignorance,
they are conjoined with birth.
The mind produced by delusion conceives of "I" and "mine," and is thus able to give rise to four types of abiding characteristics: namely,
self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), and self-pride (*ātma-māna*).
These four conditions arise from the characteristic of arising (*jāti*).
They are able to produce the mind and mental factors, causing them to reach the stage of stability; because they cause [the mind] to abide, they are called the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti*).
These four exist in the seventh consciousness.
Regarding the six distinct characteristics:
ignorance is conjoined with that characteristic of abiding.
Failing to realize that what is conceptualized as "self" and "mine" is empty,
one is thereby able to give rise to six types of discordant characteristics,
namely: greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and views.
As the Xinlun (New Treatise) states:
"The intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva consists of only six kinds.
Ignorance is in conjunction with these six kinds."
Because it can cause the abiding mind to reach a different state and direct itself outward toward objects of perception,
it is called the "differentiating characteristic."
These six pertain to the arising consciousness.
Regarding the seventh characteristic, cessation:
ignorance combines with these dissimilar characteristics.
Failing to perceive that external objects are devoid of the nature of being either agreeable or disagreeable,
one thereby gives rise to the seven types of signs of cessation,
namely the sevenfold unwholesome karma of body and speech.
These seven factors can extinguish the divergent mind that leads one into the evil realms; therefore,
they are called the "characteristics of extinction."
Just as the characteristic of cessation in the Hīnayāna school causes the present mind to cease and enter the past,
the meaning of the characteristic of cessation in the Mahāyāna is likewise.
Therefore, one should know that the four characteristics arise and the single mind flows on.
All things arise from fundamental ignorance;
although the four phases are distinguished from the subtle to the manifest in a gradual progression,
from beginning to end they are ultimately without before or after.
However, these four are neither one nor many in terms of coarse or subtle;
they are fused into a single mind.
Therefore, it is said that they exist simultaneously, yet none possess independent self-existence.
For those who have not yet exhausted the source,
awakening occurs earlier or later according to the depth of their practice.
One who has realized the source of the mind perceives the four phases of a single thought simultaneously,
as the Sūtra says:
Bodhisattvas know the end but do not know the beginning;
only the Buddha-Tathāgata knows both the beginning and the end.
"Beginning" refers to the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
The remaining three are ultimately [empty].
Since they arise through the power of ignorance,
they give rise to various dream-like thoughts.
Stirring the source of the mind,
it turns toward the mark of cessation;
one then slumbers long within the three realms.
This refers to the transmigration through the six destinies.
The four characteristics discussed above are explained in terms of the meaning of transmigration;
they correspond to the intrinsically pure awakened mind (prakṛti-prabhāsvara) as it follows along with defilement.
The five mental factors, the three subtleties, the six coarsenesses,
and so forth, are also included within this meaning.
Second is the gate of returning to the source.
This summarizes the four aspects of awakening to illustrate the meaning of initial awakening; herein,
first the general and then the specific are presented.
"Totality" refers to these four characteristics of the evolving flow;
it is the power of the inconceivable perfuming of the causal original enlightenment that gives rise to the mind of seeking and wearying detachment.
Furthermore, the teachings heard as outflows from True Suchness (tathatā) permeate the original enlightenment (mūla-awakening);
because their essence is identical and their functions are harmoniously integrated.
Having heard this, the power of the nature of understanding, nurtured by the benefits of the熏習 (vāsanā),
diminishes ignorance and gradually moves toward the source of the mind,
where the signs of cessation first begin to subside.
The marks of arising came to rest,
and he attained a brilliant, great awakening;
he realized that the source of the awakened mind is fundamentally unmoving.
It causes the beginningless quiescence to be equal and perfectly equal, such that there is no difference from beginningless awakening.
The treatise says:
"Because initial awakening is identical to fundamental awakening."
As it is said in the "Chapter on the Three Bodies" of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:
"For example, suppose there is a person who,
while in a dream..."
He saw a great river that was sweeping over and drenching his body;
he moved his hands and stirred his feet.
They cross over by cutting off the stream and reach the other shore,
because their body and mind are free from indolence.
Having awakened from the dream,
one no longer perceives the water or the distinction between this shore and the other;
yet this does not mean that the mind is absent.
Once the delusive appearances of birth and death have been extinguished,
this awareness is pure;
it does not mean that there is no awareness.
As for the distinction: this wisdom of initial awakening (ādi-bodhi-jñāna) receives four names according to its respective stages.
First, although it is awakening...
This refers to the wisdom that perceives the dream-like nature of the signs of cessation within the ten stages.
Prior to entering the ten levels of faith,
one does not know that the two types of karma— wholesome and unwholesome— necessarily bring about their corresponding two types of retribution, wholesome and unwholesome.
Only upon entering this stage does one finally awaken; therefore,
it is called "Awakening despite [the lack of prior] awakening."
Yet they still do not know that the characteristic of cessation is a dream,
nor have they awakened to the Bodhisattva;
therefore, it is called non-awakening.
Second is the awakening of similarity,
which refers to bodhisattvas and followers of the two vehicles during the stage of the three types of worthies,
because they have attained entry into the contemplation of emptiness.
The Bodhisattva is able to extinguish the conceptualization of internal and external selves and what belongs to the self, as well as greed, hatred, views, and attachment;
as the treatise says:
"One abandons the coarse conceptualization of signs of clinging."
It is like remaining asleep within a dream-image; furthermore, one has not yet reached the stage of realization.
Moreover, because the followers of the Two Vehicles have not yet fully understood the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), it is called "semblance-awakening."
Third is partial awakening,
which refers to the stages from the first bhūmi through the ninth bhūmi;
it is the awakening to the dream-like nature of the four modes of abiding.
Although this bodhisattva, by knowing that all phenomena are merely consciousness, does not give rise to coarse grasping or discrimination regarding things external to the mind,
yet after emerging from meditative equipoise,
[he perceives] the phenomena manifested within his own mind.
One still gives rise to conceptual discriminations that grasp at the dharmas of defilement and purity;
however, through non-conceptual wisdom, one attains awakening to the characteristic of abiding,
and upon reflecting back upon this characteristic of abiding, one finds that ultimately nothing exists.
Therefore, it is said that awakening abides in non-abiding, free from conceptualization and coarse thought,
and so forth. Regarding these four characteristics of abiding,
they are each abandoned one by one in the first, seventh, eighth, and ninth stages respectively.
It is like a dream arising while one is asleep;
because awakening has not yet reached fulfillment,
it is called "partial awakening."
Fourth is ultimate awakening.
This is the awakening to the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*).
This stage consists of two moments.
Therefore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"The ultimate path refers to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
This is of two kinds."
This refers to that which is subsumed under the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
whereby all movement of thought within this stage is completely exhausted.
Because the mind is focused on a single object,
it is said that the mind has no initial characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The movement of the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) is the most subtle within all moments of thought.
This is called subtle mindfulness;
it is the very moment of arising,
at which point true nature is revealed.
Therefore, it is said that one "sees the nature of the mind.
In the preceding stages,
awakening has not yet reached the source.
It is like the appearance of birth in a dream;
it moves that pure mind and brings about the karmic consciousness and so forth.
Arising and ceasing do not abide;
now this phase of birth has ended like a dream,
and the wind of ignorance has ceased.
The waves of the ocean of nature subside,
and it remains profoundly still and eternally abiding;
therefore, it is said that one attains the vision of the mind-nature, and the mind is itself eternally abiding.
Previously, my mind was not yet focused on the source;
my dream-like thoughts were not yet exhausted,
and I sought to extinguish this movement.
I have long aspired to reach the other shore;
now that all dreams and thoughts have utterly ceased,
I have awakened to the original source of the mind.
Fundamentally there is no transmigration;
contemplate the quiescence of the beginningless,
always remaining single-mindedly.
It is equal and equal;
from the beginning it has not differed from the source.
Therefore, it is called ultimate awakening.
If explained in general terms,
it is as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:
"In reliance upon the various paths of subduing."
The mind that initiates activity ceases;
by relying on the path of abandonment,
the fundamental mind ceases.
By means of the path of supreme extraction,
the fundamental mind is exhausted;
this refers to all paths of subduing.
This is called the stage of the worthy (*ārya*).
As for the cessation of the mind that initiates activity,
it is as stated in this very treatise.
The abandonment of coarse conceptualization and so forth is precisely the cessation of differentiated characteristics;
it is the path that severs phenomena.
This refers to the stage of the Dharmakāya.
Regarding "depending on the cessation of the fundamental mind," it is as stated in this treatise:
Having abandoned coarse conceptualization,
one abides in the cessation of signs;
this is the path of supreme extraction.
The adamantine mind-concentration (*vajracitta-samādhi*).
Regarding "the fundamental mind being exhausted":
in this treatise, this refers to the departure from subtle conceptualization (*sūkṣma-smṛti*).
This refers to the exhaustion of the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
Question:
How can the four characteristics coexist at the same time?
If they occur simultaneously,
how can one perceive them as preceding or succeeding?
Answer:
The mind of a dream is singular;
the four phases flow and turn.
This is the state of one dwelling within a dream.
That is to say, they are distinguished as earlier and later,
each according to the power of their wisdom,
differentiated by the depth or shallowness of their realization.
However, the Greatly Awakened One knows that the four characteristics of a dream are but a single pure mind,
entirely devoid of sequential temporal nature or substantial essence.
Therefore, it is said that at the same time there is no self-establishment and so forth.
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"In a dream, one may think many years have passed."
Awakening occurs in a mere instant;
thus, although time is immeasurable,
it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa.
In this context, a single moment is precisely non-conceptualization.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra* states:
"All phenomena are unarisen."
I teach the meaning of the moment:
that what is first born immediately perishes;
this is not taught for the sake of the foolish.
The commentary states:
That which flows and transforms moment by moment must necessarily lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is non-arising; if there were intrinsic nature, there would be no transmigration.
Therefore, it is only by realizing non-arising that one perceives the momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
The above has explained the meaning of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) according to the gate of returning to the source.
Now, [the meaning of] original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) [will be discussed].
Within this, there are two kinds:
first, the fundamentally awakened mind that conforms to defilement;
second, the fundamentally awakened mind that is intrinsically pure.
The first and second [stages] also have two aspects.
First is the characteristic of the purity of wisdom,
which refers to the characteristic of original enlightenment returning to purity in accordance with defilement.
Second is the characteristic of inconceivable activity,
which refers to the characteristic of the functional operation of the returning-to-purity fundamental awakening.
If these two are separated from defiled conditions...
Thus, it cannot be established.
Therefore, it is said that [the nature] conforms to defilement.
In the initial practice of purity, there is both cause and fruit.
The "cause" refers to the power of internal permeation by True Suchness (tathatā),
serving as the internal cause; together with the external condition of the teachings of permeating hearing that flow from True Suchness,
this pertains to the stage prior to the Grounds (bhūmi).
Relying on the power of this perfuming,
one cultivates the roots of goodness consisting of the provisions and preparatory practices;
having thus ascended to the ten stages (bhūmi).
Because one practices and realizes according to the principle,
it is called "practicing in accordance with reality.
When the practices of the ten stages are fulfilled, [one attains the fruit].
Because the vajra cause is ultimate,
it is said that the skillful means are fulfilled.
Within the fruit, there are likewise two.
This refers to the fruit of abandonment and the fruit of knowledge.
Regarding the former, through the preceding preparatory means,
one is able to destroy the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the composite consciousness.
This reveals its nature of being neither arising nor ceasing.

As for the "conjoined consciousness," it refers to the Tathāgata’s non-arising and non-ceasing [consciousness] conjoining with the seven evolving consciousnesses that are subject to arising and ceasing.
It is called the "synthesizing consciousness" (saṃghāta-vijñāna), which is the ālaya-vijñāna;
within it, fundamental ignorance (mūla-avidyā) is exhausted.
Therefore, there is nothing with which it can be conjoined;
this reveals the meaning of the dharmakāya’s original enlightenment (prakṛti-awakening).
Hence, it is called the "fruit of cessation."
As for the fruit of wisdom:
because this Dharma-body is manifested,
one is able to extinguish the characteristics of the continuity of karmic signs and so forth within the defiled mind.
At that time, the mind of original enlightenment (prakṛti-viśuddha-ālayavijñāna), following along with its defilements,
immediately returns to the source of the mind,
becoming the quiescent, pure, and perfect wisdom.
This establishes the meaning of the initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) of the response body (saṃbhoga-kāya);
therefore, it is called the "fruit of wisdom.
Nevertheless, it does not extinguish the substance of the continuous mind.
It merely extinguishes the characteristics of the continuous mind;
this intention is to clarify that by destroying the characteristics of ignorance within the synthetic consciousness,
one can manifest the principle of original enlightenment.
The characteristic of the continuous mind, such as the characteristics of extinguished karma and so forth,
is transformed into the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣāntijñāna*).
This is the second, the inconceivable characteristic of activity (*acintyakarmalakṣaṇa*).

This refers to the functioning of the two bodies— the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)— which arise from the essence and characteristics of the aforementioned original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).
These are constantly present for sentient beings as the objects of the six sense faculties.
Therefore, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"The bodies of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
are like space, devoid of marks."
For the sake of all supreme wise ones,
he creates the objects of the six sense faculties and manifests subtle and wondrous forms.
They produce sublime sounds,
causing the fragrance of the Buddha’s precepts to spread and bestowing the flavor of the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma.
One then perceives the touch of samādhi,
which causes one to know the profound and wondrous Dharma;
therefore, it is called the "wondrous realm."
Knowing that the Tathāgata is precisely for the sake of the supreme wise ones,
he establishes the objects of the six sense-fields.
This is explained through four distinct propositions.
First, the horizontal perspective reveals the qualities of karma,
which are vast, numerous, and immeasurable.
Second, the vertical perspective reveals the characteristics of karma.
Profoundly exhausting the limits of the future;
third, it reveals the excellence of its activity:
being able to respond to the capacities of beings spontaneously and without effort.
Fourth, it reveals the excellence of the activity:
its benefit is not in vain;
this refers precisely to the two bodies, the retribution body (*vipākakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The Great Function of True Suchness is without beginning and without end,
continuing in uninterrupted succession.
Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"The response body (nirmāṇakāya) has continued in succession without interruption throughout beginningless birth and death;
it is the unique quality (āveṇika-dharma) of all Buddhas."
Because it is able to sustain and uphold [the teachings],
sentient beings will never be exhausted,
nor will its function ever be exhausted.
Therefore, it is said to be eternally abiding.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"What is the accomplishment of one's own benefit?"
That is to say, one attains liberation,
becomes free from the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance to knowledge,
and achieves the unobstructed, pure body.
What is the accomplishment of the benefit of the emanation body?
Having already attained the accomplishment of benefiting oneself through one's own body since beginningless time.
One is able, by relying upon those two kinds of Buddha-bodies,
to manifest the sovereign power of practice within the world.
Question:
If one first attains self-benefit and only thereafter undertakes the activity of benefiting others,
for what purpose is it said that [the practice of] benefiting others has no beginning?
Answer:
There are two explanations.
One says:
The Tathāgata responds universally to the three periods of time in a single thought-moment;
because that which is to be responded to is beginningless,
that which is able to respond is likewise beginningless.
It is like a single moment of perfect wisdom that universally penetrates the boundless realms of the three periods of time;
for these realms are boundless.
Wisdom is also boundless.
Because it is the manifestation of boundless wisdom,
it is without beginning or end.
This is not something that can be measured by the mind or consciousness.
Second, it is said:
because ignorance has been exhausted.
Initial awakening is identical to original awakening;
yet that initial awakening has, from time immemorial,
constantly engaged in the activity of arising karma.
Because it benefits sentient beings;
because all Buddhas are without distinction;
and because there is neither new nor old.
All are without the distinction of initial awakening,
for they are fundamentally equal and without beginning or end; thus,
they are able to transform sentient beings.
This is the functioning of True Suchness;
therefore, it is called the inconceivable karma.
This functioning and the minds of sentient beings—
Fundamentally, there is no duality;
however, because one fails to awaken and follows the current, the function [of the original nature] does not manifest.
Instead, the deluded mind engages in the function of aversion and seeking.
It manifests immediately according to the faculties within the mind,
yet one does not intentionally form the thought, "I am manifesting these distinctions";
therefore, it is called "spontaneous."
The second is the intrinsically pure fundamental awakening (*prakṛtiviśuddha-mūlābodhi*);
this refers to the characteristic of the essence of awakening.
Now, it will be explained that within this there are both general and specific aspects.
As for "pervasive," it means that this awakened nature does not abide in its own nature; thus,
although it follows various conditions to become either defiled or pure.
Yet it never loses its intrinsically pure nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
Because this pure nature is not lost,
it is able to manifest as either defiled or pure in accordance with conditions.
It is like a bright mirror that manifests both defiled and pure phenomena;
although it manifests the defiled and the pure,
it never loses the luminous purity of the mirror itself.
Because the clarity of the mirror is not lost,
it can manifest the appearances of both defilement and purity; through these appearances of defilement and purity,
one knows that the clarity of the mirror is pure.
By means of the purity of the mirror's appearance, one knows the manifestation of defilement and purity;
yet, although pure phenomena appear,
they do not increase the clarity of the mirror.
Although defiled phenomena appear within it,
they do not defile the purity of the mirror; moreover,
it is not merely that they do not defile it.
Furthermore, it is precisely by means of this that the clarity and purity of the mirror are revealed by contrast;
one should know that fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is likewise so.
It is not merely that its immovable, intrinsically pure nature constitutes both defilement and purity.
Furthermore, it is only through the accomplishment of defilement and purity that the intrinsic purity of nature manifests; therefore,
it is the intrinsically enlightened mind (prakṛti-vijñāna) that conforms to defilement.
The intrinsically pure original enlightenment (prakṛtiviśuddha-mūlābodhi) encompasses its entirety;
it is a single nature without duality.
An alternative interpretation is that these four kinds of mirrors serve as metaphors for this fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).
First is the mirror of emptiness,
which means being devoid of the substance of all external objects.
Second is the mirror of non-emptiness.
This means that the substance of a mirror is inherently capable of manifesting all images.
Third is the "pure mirror," which refers to one that has been polished and cleansed of impurities.
Fourth is the mirror for enjoyment,
which is placed upon a high platform;
those who require it may use it.
Among the four [purities], the first two are purity by nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*),
while the latter two are purity through the removal of stains (*vaimalya-viśuddhi*).
Furthermore, the first two are explained with reference to the period when the cause is latent.
The latter two are explained in terms of time as manifested through the fruit.
Furthermore, the former two concern emptiness and non-emptiness,
while the latter two concern essence and function.
Furthermore, the first two constitute the essence and the latter two the characteristics;
thus it is said that they are the "essence and characteristics of awakening."
Because the essence of the mind is simply the absence of non-awakening,
it is called "original awakening" (benjue);
because the essence of the mind possesses the function of awakening and illumination, it is so named.

Therefore, it is called "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*). If one were to claim that it is called "original enlightenment" simply because there is no "non-enlightenment," then by the same logic,
it would also follow that it is "non-enlightenment" because there is no "enlightened illumination."
If that which possesses awakening and illumination is called "original awakening" (mūla-bodhi),
it is not yet known whether this awakening cuts off delusions or not. If it does not cut off delusions, [how can it be called original awakening?]
There would then be no function of awakening and illumination;
if delusions were severed,
there would be no ordinary beings.
Answer:
It is not merely that there is no darkness;
there is also luminous illumination.
Because there is clear illumination,
the establishment of the severance of delusions exists.
What is the meaning of this?
If one defines "awakening" based on being awake after having previously slept,
then initial awakening (shijue) would exist while fundamental awakening (benjue) would be non-existent.
If awakening is defined by being originally without sleep,
then original awakening (benjue) is awakening,
whereas initial awakening (shijue) is not.
The meaning of "severance" (prahāṇa) is likewise.
That which was previously existent and subsequently becomes non-existent is called severance;
thus, initial enlightenment (ādikṣānti-jñāna) possesses severance.
Original enlightenment is without cessation.
If that which is primordially free from delusion were called "cessation," then original enlightenment itself would be cessation.
Initial awakening is uninterrupted.
If one relies on this meaning,
because it has been fundamentally severed, there have fundamentally been no ordinary beings.
Therefore, the Treatise says:
"All sentient beings have, from the very beginning, entered the dharma of nirvāṇa and bodhi.
Although there has been no ordinary person from the outset, [they have always been enlightened].
Yet, because there has never been initial awakening,
there have always been ordinary beings from the very beginning.
Question:
If this original enlightenment serves as the cause for both the defiled and the pure,
or if it serves as the cause for pure phenomena alone—
should it be the cause for pure phenomena alone?
Why does the sutra state that the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome?
If it universally functions as the nature of both defilement and purity,
why is it said to possess only virtuous qualities?
It does not state that its nature is defiled or afflicted.
Answer:
This principle applies universally because it serves as the nature for both defilement and purity.
It is taught that it possesses intrinsic virtuous qualities;
that is to say, because the principle is free from impure dharmas,
it is able to produce all defiled dharmas in accordance with conditions.
Furthermore, because it is by nature free from defilement,
it is able to produce all pure phenomena according to conditions. Since it can produce both the defiled and the pure,
[it is called the "all-encompassing"].
It serves as the nature of both defilement and purity;
because it is free from the natures of defilement and purity,
it is said to possess only the qualities of its own nature.
Because one attains the nature of freedom from defilement and purity,
all merits are thereby perfected; thus,
one adopts and abandons the natures of defilement and purity.
This is because they are all merely false appearances.
Question:
Within the previously mentioned "fundamental awakening that accords with defilement,"...
What is the distinction between the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi*) and this dharma?
Furthermore, what is the distinction between the previously mentioned inconceivable karma (*acintya-karman*) and this perfuming by conditions (*pratyaya-vāsanā*)?
Answer:
Because it was previously explained that [the mind] follows defilement,
its return to purity is described as "wisdom" (jñāna);
this clarifies the functional activity of that wisdom.
This refers only to initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*).
Since this pertains to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
it reveals the essence of the Dharma by being free from hindrances.
This clarifies the function of this dharma;
it is explained solely in terms of the essence of the dharma.
Therefore, it was previously called "wisdom" (jñāna).
This is called "dharmas";
what was previously called "karma" is here called "conditions."
The meaning of the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing is also called the "five meanings.
Briefly, there are four gates [to its exposition].
First, the explanation of the names and meanings;
second, the presentation of the essential nature and characteristics;
third, the extensive elucidation of the intent.
Fourth, the resolution of doubts through questions and answers.
First, regarding the brief explanation:
as for the causal conditions, the *ālaya*—the substance of the mind—does not maintain its own nature.
This is the cause of arising and ceasing.
External, delusive objects stir up waves of consciousness;
this is the condition for arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, the substance of the mind serves as the cause,
while within the two meanings of the ālayavijñāna, the meaning of non-awakening serves as the condition.
Based upon these two meanings...
This is to reveal that all consciousnesses arise and perish through causes and conditions,
being produced by the gathering of their characteristics.
Therefore, they are called "sentient beings," yet they have no separate essence;
they exist solely in dependence upon the substance of the mind.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"Because it evolves in dependence upon mind, thought, and consciousness.
This clarifies the essence of the mind.
This mind, which is the supported basis (āśraya),
is itself that which supports (āśrita).
"Transformation" (parāvṛtti) means arising.
"Depending on the mind" indicates the cause.
"Depending on the ālayavijñāna" clarifies that within the mind, ignorance possesses both the causes and conditions.
Among the five kinds of mentation,
the first three exist in the state of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
while the latter two exist in the state of the subtle divisions of the phenomenal consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
Within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
if discussed in detail,
there are four kinds of consciousness.
First is the true consciousness;
it is also called the self-characteristic and also called the wisdom-characteristic.
Second is the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*),
also called the phase of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) or the consciousness of the phase of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna*).
The three evolving consciousnesses are also called "evolving characteristics" and are also called "evolving-characteristic consciousnesses."
The fourth is the manifest consciousness (*pratyakṣa-vijñāna*);
it is also called the manifest aspect (*pratyakṣa-nimitta*) and the manifest-aspect-consciousness (*pratyakṣa-nimitta-vijñāna*).
The five consciousnesses are also called the "characteristic of cognition.
The sixth is the "continuing consciousness."
It is also called the characteristic of continuity.
As for the initial true consciousness,
it does not depend on anything else for its establishment.
The characteristic of wisdom is the nature of cognitive illumination.
As for the karmic consciousness:
Arising from stillness and moving:
as for the evolving consciousnesses,
they proceed from within toward the outside.
The manifesting consciousness arises from the manifestation of objects;
the cognitive consciousness is that which cognizes them.
Regarding the continuity [of existence], which discriminates between defilement and purity based on delusive objects,
it relies upon various karmic causes.
The fruit of suffering is not severed.
Because these six categories represent the essential substance,
they are collectively termed "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).
Each possesses its own spiritual discernment (*vijñāna*),
which differs from empty space; therefore,
they are collectively termed "consciousness."
Among these six meanings,
the first is the basis,
while [the remaining five] are the five that depend upon it.
Furthermore, the first [nature] serves as the basis for both the subject and the object;
moreover, the first has the meaning of being immutable,
while the latter five have the meaning of following conditions.
Furthermore, the first two [transformations] are the self-substance portion of the ālayavijñāna;
the next two are the seeing and image portions;
and the final two are the subtle portions of the phenomenal consciousness (*karmavipākavijñāna*).
Regarding the two aspects of the perceived and the perceiving,
there are two explanations concerning the *karmic consciousness* (*vastu-vijñāna*). One says:
The "active consciousness" (karmic-consciousness) refers to the six consciousnesses.
The reason this is known is that it is explained by citing external objects within the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
One explanation states:
these are the seven evolving consciousnesses;
the seventh is also associated with the mental factor of wisdom (*mati*).
Because it takes external objects as its conditions.
The reason for this knowledge is stated in the *Furen jing* (Sutra on the Woman):
Regarding the knowledge of these six consciousnesses and mental factors:
these seven phenomena do not abide for even a single moment.
As for the phrase "knowledge of mental factors":
This is precisely the factor of wisdom.
Furthermore, in the context of the "Golden Drum" parable,
it states that the mental faculty discriminates all phenomena and so forth.
As for this substance of the mind:
these five functions, in relation to various objects,
are able to give rise to mental consciousness.
Among these, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is the sixth;
it refers exclusively to that which arises subsequent to birth.
In terms of its meaning, however, it is universally subsumed within the category of mental consciousness.
Second, regarding the essential nature:
generally, it takes the single mind as its essence;
if discussed specifically, however—
The essence of its own-characteristic is precisely original enlightenment;
it is not a characteristic of movement or transformation.
This is the nature of awakening and illumination.
Therefore, the Treatise states:
"The meaning of awakening refers to the essence of mind being free from thought."
That which is free from the marks of discursive thought is equal to the realm of empty space;
there is nowhere it does not pervade.
The dharma-realm is of a single mark.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal dharma-body.
Based on this dharma-body, it is termed "original enlightenment" (mūla-awakening).
As for the essence of the karma-consciousness:
This refers to the essence of the originally enlightened mind,
which, due to the wind of ignorance,
remains entirely unmoving in its entirety.
The characteristic of immovability has not yet turned toward external objects,
like a slight ripple on the ocean.
It is quiescent and without movement;
yet, it does not transfer from this place to another.
Such is the nature of the evolving consciousnesses.
This means that based on ignorance and the consciousness of karma,
there is a functional capacity for seeing that arises directed outwardly.
Yet it has not yet manifested the aspect of the object of perception;
it is like the coarse waves of the ocean, which depend on the power of the wind and subtle movement, and from this,
they are stirred and driven forth.
It arises through transference.
This has two meanings.
If, with respect to that which is moved by ignorance, it becomes the "seer," [then it is as follows].
Within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
if it is moved by objects and becomes the perceiver,
this occurs within the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
This refers here to the initial [stage].
As for the essence of the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*),
it means that it is able to see by virtue of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Once the objective realm has manifested,
the seer and the seen are both fully present,
just as coarse waves on the ocean arise due to the power of the wind.
The characteristics of the myriad phenomena are not one, but manifold.
If one discusses them in terms of their general characteristics,
they revolve through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) by means of karma.
Because this is a transformative characteristic,
and because it is not a transformation into quiescence,
there is wisdom within karma.
Because the mind of original enlightenment moves as its entire substance,
this wisdom also permeates the evolving consciousnesses;
for within the midst of such movement and transformation, the nature of understanding remains indestructible.
This consciousness is also termed "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa);
for characteristics such as karma are not the fundamental characteristic of the mind,
but arise due to ignorance.
It may be called "other-characterized," for it does not move by its own nature,
but moves in accordance with others.
Among these, the nature of understanding is the intrinsic nature of the mind;
because it is not established by depending on anything else,
it is called its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
In this way, these specific characteristics also apply to the seven consciousnesses,
because these [consciousnesses] are transformations of that mind; thus,
it is also these seven consciousnesses.
This is precisely the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
because it does not lose its spiritual understanding.
Furthermore, the two evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are solely the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
This karmic consciousness is solely the consciousness of the aspect of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna*),
because apart from fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), it has no separate substance.
As for the essence of the *jñāna-vijñāna* (consciousness of cognition), it is a subtle subdivision within the *vastu-vijñāna* (consciousness of things).
This is because it does not discern the false objects manifested within the presently appearing consciousness.
The essence of the continuous consciousness (*saṃtānavijñāna*), which is capable of giving rise to subtle discriminations of defilement and purity,
is also within the empirical consciousness (*saviṣayavijñāna*).
"Subtle" refers to that which is associated with the clinging to dharmas;
"long-lasting" means obtaining continuity.
This is in terms of its own essence being uninterrupted.
To explain the meaning of continuity:
this consciousness is able to give rise to the afflictions that initiate karma and moisten rebirth;
it is also able to draw forth and maintain the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma—the various formations (*saṃskāra*)—originated by past ignorance.
This causes it to become a state of existence capable of producing results;
for if there were no afflictions to moisten karma,
the seeds would wither and perish.
This refers to that which draws forth and brings to maturity;
furthermore, it can give rise to the maturation of karma, afflictions, and retribution for Bodhisattvas who moisten their rebirths.
In this way, the causal flow through the three periods of time continues without interruption;
this achievement is due to the mental consciousness.
Third, to explain its meaning in detail:
the initial karma-consciousness is the first of the three subtleties.
It is the first among the four characteristics and the sixth among the six defilements;
that is to say, fundamental ignorance is non-accumulation.
Karmic consciousness is without suffering;
yet, being without suffering, it is never for a moment separated from the accumulation [of karma].
Nevertheless, although this karmic consciousness undergoes arising and ceasing, it remains thus.
It is most subtle;
subject and object are not yet differentiated.
Ignorance is likewise so.
Therefore, the *Nirābhāsa-śāstra* asks:
"What are the characteristics and what is the object of this consciousness?"
Answer:
The characteristic and its object cannot be distinguished;
they are of one essence and without difference.
Question:
If that is so, how is it known that they exist?
Answer:
Because of the knowledge of phenomena, this consciousness exists;
consciousness is able to give rise to all afflictions, karma, and the phenomena of retribution.
It is like ignorance, which constantly arises.
Can this ignorance be conceptually differentiated?
If it can be differentiated,
it cannot be called ignorance.
If one does not engage in conceptual discrimination,
then it may be said that it is non-existent;
yet it is existent and not non-existent.
Furthermore, just as ignorance is known to exist by means of desire, hatred,
and so forth, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is likewise understood in this way.
The same is stated in the Abhidharma-piṭaka-sūtra.
These passages specifically refer to the karma-consciousness (karma-vijñāna);
the meanings regarding the other consciousnesses are too extensive to detail here.
Therefore, for now, do not be attached;
it can be understood through inference.
As for the fourth question and answer:
Question:
For what reason are the five consciousnesses not mentioned?
Answer:
This treatise speaks according to a single meaning;
it intends only to explain the solitary conceptualization of the six sense objects.
Therefore, the treatise says:
The various false attachments that follow after objects and conditions,
discriminating among the six sense-fields,
are called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It is also called the "discriminating consciousness," because it relies upon the six sense organs to separately apprehend the six sense objects.
Furthermore, as for the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness), it is so called because it can differentiate various phenomena such as those of the past and future, or the internal and external.
Question: [What is this?]
By what causes do these five intentions arise?
Answer:
Only through the conjunction of the real and the false do the two causes arise; thus,
the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
The inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation, Mahāmati,
are the causes of the manifesting consciousness.
Grasping at various objects and the perfuming of the beginningless deluded mind constitute the cause of the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness that discriminates phenomena).
The commentary explains:
The root and the branch constitute the two causes.
Regarding "inconceivable perfuming," it is ignorance that performs the perfuming.
True Suchness (tathatā) cannot be perfumed or received, yet it is capable of perfuming;
therefore, where there is perfuming, it is never exhausted.
This is the perfuming that is inexhaustible.
This is called "inconceivable perfuming.
Regarding "inconceivable transformation," it refers to the mind of true suchness receiving the perfuming of ignorance.
That which is immutable undergoes transformation;
yet transformation is itself non-transformation.
This non-transformation is called the inconceivable.
However, this perfuming and transformation are extremely profound and subtle;
therefore, the manifest consciousness that arises from them has extremely fine and minute characteristics.
Within this, there are also the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*);
since the coarse is cited to include the subtle,
it simply says that the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*) grasps various objects.
These very various objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness (ālayavijñāna) in turn stir the ocean of the mind,
giving rise to the waves of the active consciousness (pravṛttivijñāna).
"Perfumed by beginningless delusive conceptualization" refers to the arising of the habitual tendencies of delusive thoughts within that ocean of the combined mind;
perfumed since beginningless time, this habituation continues without interruption.
Because one has not yet abandoned discursive thought,
these coarsenesses and thoughts perfume and stir the ocean of the mind.
Because various consciousnesses arise through the manifestation of deluded thought and coarse objects,
the activity-consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that is produced has coarse and manifest characteristics.
The mind associated with the characteristics of formation intends to manifest the evolving consciousness;
it arises based on inconceivable perfuming and abides based on inconceivable transformation.
The active consciousness arises depending on objects and abides depending on the ocean of mind;
this is what is explained in this treatise.
It speaks only of the conditions for arising and does not discuss the basis of abiding; therefore,
within the subtle [level], it mentions only the permeation by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Among the coarse [factors], this alone mentions the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, when birth abides in its ground,
the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) arises with ignorance (*avidyā*) as its cause.
By means of karma, one abides in the stages;
with ignorance as the cause, the consciousness of phenomena arises.
Furthermore, the ten-fascicle sutra says:
There are four kinds of causes by which the eye and so forth arise and so on.
Question:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises state that the ālayavijñāna is the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) which is exclusively subject to arising and ceasing.
Why, then, does this treatise say that it contains both meanings?
Answer:
Each has its own description,
and they do not contradict one another;
that is to say, this subtle mind.
Briefly, there are two meanings.
From the perspective of its being ripened by ignorance,
it perfumes the quiescent [mind] and causes it to move.
Movement and stillness are of one essence.
This present treatise relies upon the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra.
To remedy the attachment to the distinct substantiality of the ultimate and the conventional,
it is taught that the unarisen and undying is conjoined with the arisen and dying, being neither identical nor different.
Furthermore, there is no differentiation between the sovereign and its attributes, nor is there any correspondence with external objects.
It also possesses both the awakened and the unawakened aspects.
If one discusses the sense of being induced by karma and afflictions, it is distinguished as non-existent,
yet it causes there to be exclusively arising and ceasing.
In the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other such treatises,
in order to eliminate the views that [the self] is permanent and unitary,
it is taught that this consciousness arises and ceases exclusively as a distinct continuum of mind and mental factors.
However, although these two intentions differ— this being induced by karma and afflictions,
and that being moved by ignorance—
[they are nonetheless connected].
The substance of consciousness is non-dual.
Question:
Is the substance of the mind eternally abiding, or is it subject to arising and ceasing?
This refers to the arising and ceasing of the mind's manifestations;
because essence and manifestation are unified as a single consciousness,
this essence of the mind is eternally abiding.
Answer:
If one has attained the realization of the meaning,
both interpretations are permitted.
If one discusses permanence,
it is called "essence" because it does not depend on others for its establishment;
if one discusses impermanence, [it is likewise].
These are the words and signs that follow along with arising and ceasing.
As for what is called "arising and ceasing," it is not the arising of arising.
It is not an extinction that extinguishes;
it is the arising and extinction of the mind itself.
Therefore, it is called "arising-extinction" (shengmie).
Therefore, it can be said that the essence of the mind arises and ceases, just as water moving is called waves;
one can never say that this movement is the movement of something other than the water.
The principle herein is likewise.
If the substance of the mind is unmoving while only the appearances of ignorance move,
then there would be no principle for transforming an ordinary person into a sage.
Because the characteristics of ignorance are unilaterally extinguished,
and because the essence of mind has never been that of an ordinary being from the outset.
Question:
If the essence of the mind were subject to arising and ceasing, then the true mind would be exhaustible,
because that which arises and ceases lacks permanence.
Answer:
Although the substance of the mind arises and ceases,
the substance of the mind is eternally abiding.
Because they are neither identical nor different,
there is no duality and no singular nature.
Movement and stillness are not one, yet they possess no distinct natures.
Therefore, like water,
it possesses movement by virtue of the continuity of its succession.
Based on the gate of arising and ceasing,
it is eternally unmoving,
because it is neither permanent nor discontinuous.
Question:
Regarding this consciousness,

the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
The ālayavijñāna manifests objects through discrimination—
the self-body, the means of subsistence, and the receptacle world—

It is not a matter of preceding or succeeding.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"This consciousness evolves by means of discerning two kinds of objects."
First, regarding the discernment of internal appropriation:
this refers to the discernment of the habitual tendencies of false attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
as well as the various material sense faculties and their physical bases.
That is to say, whether it be the realm of form or the formless realm,
there is only the discernment of the habitual tendencies of false attachment.
Second, regarding the discernment of the external, non-conceptual sign of the receptacle world:
this refers to the discernment of the ālayavijñāna, which is the internal appropriation serving as the basis;
thus, at all times and without interruption, there is the appearance of the receptacle world.
This means that, like the flame of a lamp,
at the moment of its arising, it internally assumes its function while externally emitting light.
In this way, the ālayavijñāna internally takes up the grasping of objects and externally perceives external objects.
The principle of the arising of the objective world of the vessel-realm should be understood in the same way.
As stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*:
This consciousness has four kinds of objects:
namely, the sense-field (viṣaya), the sense-organ (indriya), consciousness (vijñāna), and that which is grasped by consciousness.
Since these do not exist, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) that acts as the perceiving subject cannot arise either.
If one relies on the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and the *Laṅkāvatāra*,
then habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and so forth are not objects of this consciousness;
however, if one relies on the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The auditory object and the seven consciousnesses,
etc., are not its objects of cognition according to this treatise.
The sense faculties, consciousnesses, and so forth are likewise not the objective realms manifested by this consciousness.
Since they are thus contradictory,

Answer:
This is not contradictory;
the word "only" (eva) indicates that one takes this very dharma as an object.
It does not mention other dharmas because they are not its domain.
Question:
Although there is no contradiction,

The differing points each have their own underlying logic.
For instance, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* seeks to clarify that all phenomena as they manifest are actually manifestations of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Apart from consciousness,

therefore, it is said that only the active manifestations [of consciousness] exist.
When the seeds are not manifest,
they are indistinguishable from consciousness,
as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts.
This is to demonstrate that all phenomena lack any self-continuum apart from [the mind], and thus,
with the exception of the mind and mental factors,
all other phenomena of external continua are excluded.
All these are what this consciousness cognizes.
Since all minds and mental factors cannot be established apart from objects,
the meaning [of this] is self-evident.
Therefore, they are not explained separately.
The remaining cases concerning the manifestation and disappearance [of the faculties] may be understood by analogy with this.
One must not falsely cling to a single partial view and thereby slander the comprehensive teaching.
Question:
What is the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the fundamental consciousness?
If it arises solely from defiled conditions, then when those defiled phenomena are exhausted,
[it too would be exhausted]. If it were indeed to arise from defiled conditions,
then at the time when defiled dharmas cease, [it would likewise cease].
Their own characteristics are subject to extinction.
If they were not extinguished by following along with defilement,

Furthermore, if it were to cease by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),

Answer: One says.
The essence of the ālayavijñāna is a dharma of maturation (vipāka);
it arises solely through the power of karma and afflictions.
Therefore, when karma and afflictions are exhausted, [it ceases].
Although the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is suddenly exhausted,
the state of Buddhahood likewise possesses the two practices of merit and wisdom,
which give rise to the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
In these two instances,
the meaning of "mind" is identical;
for this reason, it is said that the mind reaches the fruit of Buddhahood.
One interpretation states:
The substance of the mind arises entirely from ignorance;
this is an arising in which movement and stillness are conjoined.
It is not that words can distinguish non-existence and cause this mind to exist; rather,
it arises from ignorance and functions as karma.
This moving mind is fundamentally the mind itself;
this is termed the "gate of the meaning of self-characteristics."
It does not arise from ignorance;
furthermore, because this moving mind also possesses its own kind of mutual production and cessation,

Yet there is the principle of non-extinction:
when ignorance is exhausted,
the characteristic of movement ceases accordingly.
The mind follows initial awakening and returns to its original source.
A commentary states:

third, questions and answers to eliminate doubts.
First, the listing of the names:
First, the defilement associated with grasping;
second, the defilement associated with non-interruption;
third, the defilement associated with discriminating cognition.
Fourth, the defilement of non-concomitance with manifested form;
fifth, the defilement of non-concomitance with the mind that perceives;
sixth, the defilement of non-concomitance with the fundamental karma.
Regarding the second [topic], the treatment and abandonment:

However, the first five [consciousnesses] are explained from the subtle to the coarse, based on the meaning of the sequential order of their arising through causes and conditions.
Now, because I wish to distinguish and explain the sequence of their cessation,
I shall speak from the coarse to the subtle.
First, regarding the defilement associated with attachment (*saṃprayoga-kleśa*):
Among these six types of coarseness,
